blocks.html: Start here Two people sat in the same office for over a year and never spoke to each other. Their desks faced opposite ways. Then they spent two days doing outdoor team games. By the end they were laughing, shouting and cheering together. That’s the power of outbound training.
blocks.text:
Start here Two people sat in the same office for
over a year and never spoke to each other. Their desks faced opposite
ways. Then they spent two days doing outdoor team games. By the end they
were laughing, shouting and cheering together. That’s the power of outbound training .

What is outbound training
(OBT)?

blocks.html: Outbound training means learning teamwork through outdoor group activities. You don’t just hear about teamwork. You do it, with your body, sweat and all.
blocks.text:
Outbound training means learning teamwork through outdoor group
activities . You don’t just hear about teamwork. You do it, with your body, sweat and all.

blocks.html: Why? In any job, you must work with other people. You need to:
blocks.text:
Why? In any job, you must work with other people .
You need to:

blocks.html:
• get along with them,
  • communicate well, and
  • bring out the group effect.
blocks.text: get along with them, communicate well, and bring out the group effect .
The group effect

blocks.html: Lecture example — Paes and Bhupathi In singles tennis, Leander Paes and Mahesh Bhupathi were ranked far from the top. When they played doubles together, they became the world’s No. 1 pair. Together, they were much stronger than each of them alone.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — Paes and Bhupathi In singles tennis, Leander Paes and Mahesh Bhupathi were
ranked far from the top. When they played doubles
together , they became the world’s No. 1 pair .
Together, they were much stronger than each of them alone.

blocks.caption:
Alone, each player is good. Together, they
become the best.

blocks.html: This is called synergy: the team’s result is more than the sum of each person’s effort.
blocks.text: This is called synergy : the team’s result is more than the sum of each person’s effort.
The buddy-carry activity

blocks.html: Lecture example — “Your buddy is injured” An IT company sent 80 staff for training. They were put in 40 pairs. The trainer said: “Your buddy is injured and can’t walk. First aid is 50 metres away. Get your buddy there.” At first nobody knew what to do. Then some carried their partner on their shoulders, some piggyback, and they ran. The running wasn’t the point. After two days, people who had never spoken were sitting together, joking and talking. They had learned they could carry each other.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — “Your buddy is injured” An IT
company sent 80 staff for training. They were put in 40
pairs . The trainer said: “Your buddy is injured and can’t walk.
First aid is 50 metres away. Get your buddy there.” At first nobody knew
what to do. Then some carried their partner on their shoulders , some piggyback , and they
ran. The running wasn’t the point. After two days, people who had never
spoken were sitting together, joking and talking . They
had learned they could carry each other .

blocks.caption:
When you carry a teammate, you build a
bond that no meeting can.

blocks.text:
What to watch for in a team
task

blocks.html:
Step What it means
Plan Decide what to do before you start.
See the resources Every person is a resource: someone tall and strong, someone small and quick. You may find hidden skills.
Beat the clock Like any project, you’re racing against time.
Mid-course correction Fix the plan while you’re doing the task.
Help the slow ones “A chain is only as strong as its weakest link.” Give a shoulder to whoever is struggling.

Step What it means Plan Decide what to do before you start. See the resources Every person is a resource: someone tall and

Three rules for the day

blocks.caption:
Wear a smile, balance
your head and heart, and stay safe.

blocks.text:
1. You’re not fully
dressed without a smile

blocks.html:
• A smile shows energy and confidence.
  • People who are confident, and have nothing to hide, smile easily.
  • It’s hard to get angry while you’re smiling.
blocks.text:
A smile shows energy and confidence . People who are confident, and have nothing to hide, smile
easily. It’s hard to get angry while you’re smiling.

2. Keep your head and heart
in place

blocks.html:
• Heart = feelings and excitement. Head = thinking and reasoning.
  • In a contest, it’s natural to get excited. That’s fine, but keep thinking clearly too.
  • Balance energy with good sense.
blocks.text: Heart = feelings and excitement. Head = thinking and reasoning. In a contest, it’s natural to get excited. That’s fine, but keep thinking clearly too. Balance energy with good sense.
3. Safety first

blocks.html:
• Physical safety: keep your body balanced. If you can’t do something, put both feet (and hands) down and get stable.
  • Mental safety: don’t mock or shout at a teammate who couldn’t do something. A hurt from the tongue heals slower than a cut.

sections.title: The A-Frame March and the Caterpillar Walk

blocks.html: Start here Picture a tall wooden frame shaped like the letter A. One teammate stands on its crossbar, high above the ground. Four others hold ropes tied to the top. The frame can only “walk” if every rope is pulled at the right moment. If one person slips, the person on top wobbles.
blocks.text:
Start here Picture a tall wooden frame shaped like
the letter A . One teammate stands on its crossbar, high
above the ground. Four others hold ropes tied to the top. The frame can
only “walk” if every rope is pulled at the right
moment. If one person slips, the person on top wobbles.
Activity 1: The A-frame march

blocks.caption:
One person rides the frame. Four
rope-holders pull in turn so the frame “walks” one leg at a
time.

blocks.html:
• A team of about six gets one A-shaped bamboo frame.
  • One person stands on the crossbar.
  • Teammates hold ropes pulling in four directions (front, back, left, right).
  • By tilting and swinging the frame, they make it step forward, leg by leg.
  • Finish rule: both legs of the frame must cross the finish line.
blocks.text:
A team of about six gets one A-shaped bamboo
frame. One person stands on the crossbar . Teammates hold ropes pulling in four
directions (front, back, left, right). By tilting and swinging the frame, they make it step
forward , leg by leg. Finish rule: both legs of the
frame must cross the finish line.

Activity 2: The caterpillar
walk

blocks.caption:
Everyone stands on the same two
planks. If you don’t move together, nobody moves.

blocks.html:
• The whole team stands on two long planks, one foot on each, in a line.
  • To move, everyone must lift the same foot at the same time.
  • One person out of step, and the whole “caterpillar” stops.
blocks.text:
The whole team stands on two long planks , one foot
on each, in a line. To move, everyone must lift the same
foot at the same time . One person out of step, and the whole “caterpillar” stops.
What the players said

blocks.html:
What they noticed The lesson
“If one person loosened the rope, the middle person couldn’t balance.” Everyone’s effort matters.
“We had different opinions, but we combined them into one plan.” Listen, then agree on one way.
“The other team finished first, but we didn’t give up.” Aim to finish the task, not just to win.
“We chose the lightest person to stand on the frame.” Pick the right person for each role.
“There was no single leader. It was a flat team.” Shared leadership can work.
The rider first struggled. Instead of being replaced, she said, “I’ll learn and do it,” and she did. Willingness to learn beats giving up.
“I didn’t even look at the other team. I was fully focused.” Be fully immersed. No distractions.

Lessons from the faculty
briefing
1. Understand the task clearly

blocks.html: Lecture example — Arjuna and the bird’s eye In the Mahabharata, the teacher Drona asks his students what they see when they aim at a wooden bird. Others say “the tree, the branch, the bird”. Arjuna says, “I see only the eye of the bird.” Be that sharp about your goal.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — Arjuna and the bird’s eye In the
Mahabharata, the teacher Drona asks his students what they see when they
aim at a wooden bird. Others say “the tree, the branch, the bird”.
Arjuna says, “ I see only the eye of the bird. ” Be that sharp about your goal.
2. Know and use your resources

blocks.html:
• Resources are materials and people.
  • Know each person’s strengths and weaknesses, then give out roles wisely.
  • Who stands on the crossbar? Who pulls the ropes?
blocks.text:
Resources are materials and people . Know each person’s strengths and weaknesses , then
give out roles wisely . Who stands on the crossbar? Who pulls the ropes?
3. Share the vision

blocks.html:
• OBT has no named leader. Even a senior manager runs alongside a new joiner. All are equal.
  • As the task goes on, someone emerges to coordinate.
  • That person must make sure everyone knows the goal.
blocks.text:
OBT has no named leader . Even a senior manager runs
alongside a new joiner. All are equal. As the task goes on, someone emerges to
coordinate. That person must make sure everyone knows the
goal .
4. Review and correct

blocks.html:
• Stop now and then to check progress.
  • Change roles, give someone a rest, swap people, like geese changing their leader.
blocks.text:
Stop now and then to check progress. Change roles, give someone a rest , swap people,
like geese changing their leader.

5. Planning time is never
wasted

blocks.html: Everyone gives ideas. The leader weighs them and picks one plan.
blocks.text:
Everyone gives ideas. The leader weighs them and picks one
plan .

blocks.html: Your idea wasn’t chosen? Drop it. Carry out the chosen plan with full energy, as if it were your own idea. That’s how a team wins.
blocks.text:
Your idea wasn’t chosen? Drop it. Carry out the
chosen plan with full energy, as if it were your own
idea. That’s how a team wins.

blocks.html: The core aim of OBT: channel everyone’s energy towards the organisation’s goals.
blocks.text: The core aim of OBT: channel everyone’s energy towards the organisation’s goals.

sections.title: What Is Teamwork, and Why Does It Matter?

blocks.html: Start here One ant can’t scare anything. One crab is easy to push around. But in the lecture videos, when ants, crabs and penguins joined together, they chased away much bigger enemies. Small and weak alone, strong together.
blocks.text:
Start here One ant can’t scare anything. One crab is
easy to push around. But in the lecture videos, when ants, crabs and
penguins joined together , they chased away much bigger
enemies. Small and weak alone, strong together.

blocks.html: TEAM = Together Everyone Achieves More.
blocks.text: TEAM = Together Everyone Achieves More.

blocks.caption:
Alone, an ant is tiny. Together,
ants carry a giant leaf and even bridge a gap with their
bodies.

blocks.text: Don’t panic. Call your team.

blocks.html:
• When danger or uncertainty comes, everyone feels fear. That’s human.
  • The first rule: don’t panic. Stay in control.
  • Alone, each creature panicked. Once friends joined in, they won.
blocks.text: When danger or uncertainty comes, everyone feels fear . That’s human. The first rule: don’t panic . Stay in control. Alone, each creature panicked. Once friends joined in, they won .
Teamwork in the real world

blocks.html:
Example What happened
Workers’ unions After the Industrial Revolution, factory workers had few rights. They joined together, chose leaders, and raised fair demands with owners.
Diversity and inclusion For years, people talked about welcoming all cultures and genders at work, but rules didn’t change. Groups of leaders kept pushing together and changed policies. Today most big companies have them.
blocks.text:
Example What happened Workers’ unions After the Industrial Revolution, factory workers had few rights.
They joined together , chose leaders, and raised fair
demands with owners. Diversity and inclusion For years, people talked about welcoming all cultures and genders at
work, but rules didn’t change. Groups of leaders kept pushing
together and changed policies. Today most big companies have
them.
Lessons from geese

blocks.caption:
Geese fly in a V: each bird gets lift from the one ahead, and the
leader keeps changing.

blocks.html: When geese migrate, they fly in a V shape. The lecture draws these lessons:
blocks.text:
When geese migrate, they fly in a V shape . The
lecture draws these lessons:

blocks.html:
What the geese do Team lesson
Each bird gets lift from the bird ahead, so the flock flies farther Working together takes less effort than working alone
A goose that leaves the V struggles to keep up Stay with the team
The lead bird changes when it gets tired Share leadership and the hard work
Birds behind honk to cheer the leader Encourage each other
If one falls sick, others stay with it Care for teammates
blocks.text:
What the geese do Team lesson Each bird gets lift from the bird ahead, so the
flock flies farther Working together takes less effort than working
alone A goose that leaves the V struggles to keep up Stay with the team The lead bird changes when it gets tired Share leadership and the hard work Birds behind honk to cheer the leader Encourage each other If one falls sick, others stay with it Care for teammates

blocks.html: The lift effect is real. Scientists have measured energy savings in birds flying in a V. The “honking to cheer” and “staying with the sick bird” parts come from a popular motivational story and haven’t been proven, but the lessons still hold.
blocks.text:
The lift effect is real. Scientists have measured energy savings
in birds flying in a V. The “honking to cheer” and “staying with the
sick bird” parts come from a popular motivational story and haven’t been
proven, but the lessons still hold.

blocks.html: Nature is full of teamwork: cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems. Planets move together in the solar system. The result is order, balance and harmony.
blocks.text:
Nature is full of teamwork: cells form tissues,
tissues form organs, organs form systems. Planets move together in the
solar system. The result is order, balance and
harmony .
Why teamwork matters

blocks.html:
• A team brings together different skills, so members complete each other.
  • Together you create synergy, which sparks new ideas and creativity.
  • Higher morale: you cheer, help, teach and even challenge each other.
  • Shared leadership and shared goals.
  • Better communication, healthy disagreement, less waste of time and money.
  • A happier workplace with more job satisfaction.
blocks.text:
A team brings together different skills , so members complete each other. Together you create synergy , which sparks new ideas and creativity. Higher morale: you cheer, help, teach and even challenge each other. Shared leadership and shared goals. Better communication, healthy disagreement, less
waste of time and money. A happier workplace with more job
satisfaction.

blocks.html: “If you want to walk fast, walk alone. If you want to walk far, walk together.” (Often credited to Ratan Tata; it’s actually an old African proverb that he liked to quote.)
blocks.text:
“If you want to walk fast, walk alone. If you want to walk far, walk
together.” (Often credited to Ratan Tata; it’s actually an old
African proverb that he liked to quote.)
Put people where they shine

blocks.html:
Lecture example — matching roles to strengths In one company, all middle managers had the same mixed duties. Nobody was excelling or enjoying the work. One-on-one talks showed three kinds of people:

  • Some loved creative work.
  • Some were great with numbers but not with people.
  • Some were great with people but not with numbers. When roles were matched to strengths, people became happier and their work got much better.

sections.title: The 10 C's of Teamwork — Clarity, Commitment, Communication

blocks.html: Start here A trekker leaves his phone on a hilltop café table. He asks a helper boy, “Can you go and have a look at my phone? Take my cycle.” Fifteen minutes later the boy returns, panting. “Sir, I saw it. It’s there.” “Then where is it?!” “You said look, not bring. And I can’t ride a cycle, so I pushed it up the hill.” Two small gaps in clarity cost a lot of time.
blocks.text:
Start here A trekker leaves his phone on a hilltop
café table. He asks a helper boy, “Can you go and have a
look at my phone? Take my cycle .” Fifteen
minutes later the boy returns, panting. “Sir, I saw it. It’s there.”
“Then where is it?!” “You said look , not bring . And I can’t ride a cycle, so I pushed it up the
hill.” Two small gaps in clarity cost a lot of time.
The 10 C’s of teamwork

blocks.caption: Ten habits that make a team work.

blocks.html:
# C # C
1 Clarity 6 Coordination
2 Commitment 7 Connection
3 Communication 8 Conflict resolution
4 Competence 9 Change management
5 Collaboration 10 Continuous improvement
blocks.text: # C # C 1 Clarity 6 Coordination 2 Commitment 7 Connection 3 Communication 8 Conflict resolution 4 Competence 9 Change management 5 Collaboration 10 Continuous improvement
C1: Clarity

blocks.html: Clarity comes first. Everyone must clearly know:
blocks.text: Clarity comes first. Everyone must clearly know:

blocks.html:
• the organisation’s vision, purpose and values,
  • their own role and how it helps the big picture,
  • each teammate’s abilities and limits.
blocks.text:
the organisation’s vision , purpose and values , their own role and how it helps the big
picture , each teammate’s abilities and limits.

blocks.html: When people see why their work matters, they feel ownership, stay motivated and are less likely to quit.
blocks.text:
When people see why their work matters, they feel ownership , stay motivated and are less
likely to quit.

blocks.html: Lecture example — the soldier at the end of the line In a war, the front can stretch for miles. Orders must reach the last soldier clearly. He must know what to do in every situation.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — the soldier at the end of the line In a war, the front can stretch for miles. Orders must reach the
last soldier clearly. He must know what to do in every
situation.

blocks.html: The ABC of communication: Accuracy, Brevity (keep it short), Clarity.
blocks.text: The ABC of communication: A ccuracy, B revity (keep it short), C larity.

blocks.html: Back to the phone story: the trekker gave unclear orders (“look”, not “bring”) and didn’t know his teammate couldn’t ride a cycle. Clear instructions are like a computer program: “Do this. If yes, then that. If not, this.”
blocks.text:
Back to the phone story: the trekker gave unclear
orders (“look”, not “bring”) and didn’t know his teammate couldn’t ride a cycle . Clear instructions are like a
computer program: “Do this. If yes, then that. If not, this.”

blocks.caption:
“Take my cycle” doesn’t help if your
teammate can’t ride one.

blocks.text: C2: Commitment

blocks.html: Commitment means a deep promise to make things happen, and going the extra mile. It starts with your promise to yourself.
blocks.text:
Commitment means a deep promise to make things
happen, and going the extra mile . It starts with your promise to yourself .

blocks.html: Lecture example — saving one run A fielder dives and stops the ball at the boundary. Two others back him up with quick throws. They save one run. In a close match, every run counts. That’s commitment.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — saving one run A fielder dives and
stops the ball at the boundary. Two others back him up with quick
throws. They save one run . In a close match, every run
counts. That’s commitment.

blocks.html: What builds commitment?
blocks.text: What builds commitment?

blocks.html:
• Shared vision and goals.
  • Clear roles: who does what, when, why and with whom.
  • Clear agreements inside the team on outcomes, deadlines and deliverables, so nobody has to guess what others expect.
  • Valuing teammates and cheering them on, like the geese.
blocks.text:
Shared vision and goals. Clear roles: who does what, when, why and with
whom. Clear agreements inside the team on outcomes,
deadlines and deliverables, so nobody has to guess what others
expect. Valuing teammates and cheering them on, like the
geese.

blocks.html: Lecture example — 100 missed calls A home helper had promised to always tell her employer by the night before if she couldn’t come. Once she couldn’t get through, so she called 100 times. There was no written contract, but she kept her word, and people trusted her for it.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — 100 missed calls A home helper had
promised to always tell her employer by the night before if she couldn’t
come. Once she couldn’t get through, so she called 100
times . There was no written contract, but she kept her word,

blocks.html: Lecture example — “Sir, I knew you would come” In a fierce battle, a section commander saw one of his soldiers dying in a nearby trench. His senior said “Don’t go, it’s too risky.” He crawled across anyway. The soldier died in his lap, saying, “Sir, I knew you would come.” Commitment to your team can be that deep.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — “Sir, I knew you would come” In a
fierce battle, a section commander saw one of his soldiers dying in a
nearby trench. His senior said “Don’t go, it’s too risky.” He crawled
across anyway. The soldier died in his lap, saying, “ Sir, I knew

blocks.html: Surface vs deep commitment:
blocks.text: Surface vs deep commitment:

blocks.html:
Surface Deep
“I’ll do the project.” Who does what? By which date? What resources?

C5: Collaboration

blocks.html: Collaboration means working together to bring out ideas, creativity and new solutions. It gives a team a big advantage.

blocks.html: How to collaborate well:
blocks.text: How to collaborate well:

blocks.html:
• The leader acts as a facilitator (a helper, not a boss) and builds psychological safety.
  • Power is shared: shared vision, goals, leadership and credit, not strict top-down orders.
  • Everyone gets an equal chance to speak, share and present.
  • It’s OK to take risks and make mistakes.
  • Icebreakers and informal events help people open up.
  • Collaboration can happen inside a team, across teams, and with clients and partners. Online tools and clear processes help.

C8: Conflict resolution

blocks.html: Conflict at work is normal: between teammates, between a lead and the team, or with a client. The lecture even says, “If there’s no conflict, something is seriously wrong.”

blocks.html: Where does conflict come from? A gap between what someone expected and what happened.

someone expected and what happened .

blocks.html: Preventing conflict:
blocks.text: Preventing conflict:

blocks.html:
• Psychological safety: a safe, non-judgmental space.
  • Open, honest, kind communication.
  • Everyone feels valued and connected.
blocks.text:
Psychological safety : a safe, non-judgmental
space. Open, honest, kind communication. Everyone feels valued and connected .

blocks.html: Resolving conflict:
blocks.text: Resolving conflict:

blocks.html:
1. Talk it out (have a dialogue).
  2. Listen actively to find the root cause.
  3. Look for a win-win solution.
  4. If needed, a fair third person steps in and looks at both sides, keeping the organisation’s good in mind.
  5. Put the team’s goal above your own or your group’s interest. Give and take.

interest. Give and take.

blocks.html: How to manage change:
blocks.text: How to manage change:

blocks.html:
• Expect resistance. People may resist or resent change at first.
  • Communicate openly to stop rumours, worry and misunderstanding.
  • Listen, ask questions, take feedback.
  • Share the big picture and any new priorities regularly.
  • Use people’s talents; let them help make decisions.
  • Have a written change plan, flexible for each kind of change.
  • Keep moving: tiny steps, big steps, but keep going.

Kaizen: the Japanese way

blocks.html: Kaizen (Japanese): kai = change, zen = good. Together: “change for the better”.
blocks.text:
Kaizen (Japanese): kai = change, zen = good. Together: “ change for the
better ”.

blocks.html:
• Everyone, from the CEO to the newest worker, looks for ways to improve.
  • Japanese companies, especially car makers, used it to get very close to zero defects.
blocks.text:
Everyone , from the CEO to the newest worker, looks
for ways to improve. Japanese companies, especially car makers , used it

blocks.html: Lecture example — the joke about defects A buyer told a Japanese supplier, “We’ll accept a few defective parts per thousand.” The supplier didn’t understand why anyone would want defects, so he made a few faulty parts separately and packed them with a note! It’s a joke, but it shows how seriously Japanese industry took quality.

so he made a few faulty parts separately and packed

How to do it

blocks.html:
• Hold brainstorming sessions to find what to improve.
  • Use short cycles with feedback built in, so you can correct course easily.
  • Break big problems into small pieces. Give each to the right people.
  • Keep upgrading your skills as the world changes.

eye); know and allocate resources; share the vision; review and correct;
planning time is never wasted; back the final plan as if it were
your own .
What is teamwork?

blocks.html:
• TEAM = Together Everyone Achieves More.
  • Small creatures together beat big ones. Don’t panic.
  • Unions and diversity and inclusion: change through togetherness.
  • Geese: uplift, rotating leader, honking encouragement, care.
  • “Walk fast alone; walk far together.”
  • Match roles to strengths.
